correctness.rationale: Independently reconstructing the geodesics, outer endpoints in the same column require the middle vertex to be absent. In different columns, an adjacent-layer pair has exactly two geodesics, with its two alternative corners as internal vertices; a far-layer pair A_i,C_j has internal pairs (A_j,B_j), (B_i,B_j), (B_i,C_i). A pivot A_i,B_i therefore precludes each possible double in another column: a second A/B double blocks A_i,B_j, a B/C double blocks A_i,C_j via B_i or B_j, and an A/C double blocks A_i,C_j via B_i or A_j. Reflection handles the other pivot. When the pivot is the only double, each pair incident with it has a clear path using the singleton endpoint's column, and all other pairs have the ordinary-column paths. Ordinary columns work because a selected outer endpoint never has its own middle vertex selected. In the ordinary class, empty columns and lone outer vertices can be extended; the all-middle set can become a pivot. When every column is middle-only or outer-paired and at least one is outer-paired, every addition makes a full column or a forbidden pivot. A pivot configuration is maximal exactly when every other column is occupied. The resulting counts give both polynomials, all maximal sizes, and the claimed unique maximum (n+1<2n for n≥2). In a separate direct BFS replay, all subsets for n=2,3,4 were checked: counts of visible/maximal sets were 41/15, 221/61 and 1137/231, and all coefficients agreed. No uploaded script was executed.
residual_risks: The bounded replay corroborates n=2,3,4 only; the geodesic classification gives the unrestricted proof.
